claim: Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) emerged globally in 2014 as a cause of acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) in children.
source: The factors leading to the global emergence of Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) in 2014 as a cause of acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) in children are unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about the timing of EV-D68 emergence.

claim: There was an approximately 50% increase in the annual probability of EV-D68 infection over the 10-year study period (2006-2017) in England.
source: Using catalytic mathematical models, we estimate an approximately 50% increase in the annual probability of infection over the 10-year study period, coinciding with the emergence of clade B around 2009.
evidence: This is based on mathematical modeling of seroprevalence data from three time points.

claim: The increase in EV-D68 transmission coincided with the emergence of clade B around 2009.
source: Using catalytic mathematical models, we estimate an approximately 50% increase in the annual probability of infection over the 10-year study period, coinciding with the emergence of clade B around 2009.
evidence: This temporal association is noted in the abstract based on the modeling results and known viral evolution.

claim: EV-D68 was already widely circulating before the AFM outbreaks.
source: Despite such increase in transmission, seroprevalence data suggest that the virus was already widely circulating before the AFM outbreaks and the increase of infections by age cannot explain the observed number of AFM cases.
evidence: This is inferred from the high seroprevalence observed in 2006, before the major AFM outbreaks.

claim: The increase in infections by age cannot explain the observed number of AFM cases.
source: Despite such increase in transmission, seroprevalence data suggest that the virus was already widely circulating before the AFM outbreaks and the increase of infections by age cannot explain the observed number of AFM cases.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing the modeled infection patterns by age with the observed AFM case distribution.

claim: The acquisition of or an increase in neuropathogenicity would be required to explain the emergence of outbreaks of AFM.
source: Therefore, the acquisition of or an increase in neuropathogenicity would be additionally required to explain the emergence of outbreaks of AFM.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the finding that transmission increases alone cannot explain AFM emergence.

claim: Changes in enterovirus phenotypes cause major changes in disease epidemiology.
source: Our results provide evidence that changes in enterovirus phenotypes cause major changes in disease epidemiology.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings regarding the relationship between viral evolution and disease patterns.

claim: EV-D68 causes severe respiratory disease and is transmitted by the respiratory route.
source: Contrary to most human enteroviruses, EV-D68 causes severe respiratory disease and is transmitted by the respiratory route, sharing properties with rhinoviruses (Oberste et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oberste et al., 2004.

claim: EV-D68 was first isolated in 1962.
source: Although this virus was first isolated in 1962, for decades it was only reported from isolated cases or small case clusters of respiratory disease (Pons-Salort et al., 2015).
evidence: This historical fact is stated with a citation to Pons-Salort et al., 2015.

claim: For decades after 1962, EV-D68 was only reported from isolated cases or small case clusters of respiratory disease.
source: Although this virus was first isolated in 1962, for decades it was only reported from isolated cases or small case clusters of respiratory disease (Pons-Salort et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pons-Salort et al., 2015.

claim: From 2009 to 2010 onwards, an increasing number of outbreaks of EV-D68-associated severe respiratory illness have been reported worldwide.
source: From 2009 to 2010 onwards however, an increasing number of outbreaks of EV-D68-associated severe respiratory illness have been reported worldwide (Holm-Hansen et al., 2016; Tokarz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holm-Hansen et al., 2016 and Tokarz et al., 2012.

claim: In 2014, the US experienced the first big outbreak of respiratory disease linked to EV-D68, with >1100 cases reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
source: In 2014, the US experienced the first big outbreak of respiratory disease linked to EV-D68, with >1100 cases reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Midgley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Midgley et al., 2015.

claim: An unusual number of acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) cases were reported in parallel with the 2014 US EV-D68 outbreak.
source: In parallel with this outbreak, an unusual number of acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) cases (a newly recognised condition that includes the sudden onset of flaccid limb weakness [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021]) were also reported, and similar AFM outbreaks subsequently occurred in 2016 and 2018 (Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to CDC 2021 and Park et al., 2021.

claim: AFM is a newly recognised condition that includes the sudden onset of flaccid limb weakness.
source: In parallel with this outbreak, an unusual number of acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) cases (a newly recognised condition that includes the sudden onset of flaccid limb weakness [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021]) were also reported, and similar AFM outbreaks subsequently occurred in 2016 and 2018 (Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This definition is supported by citation to CDC 2021.

claim: Similar AFM outbreaks occurred in 2016 and 2018.
source: In parallel with this outbreak, an unusual number of acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) cases (a newly recognised condition that includes the sudden onset of flaccid limb weakness [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021]) were also reported, and similar AFM outbreaks subsequently occurred in 2016 and 2018 (Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Park et al., 2021.

claim: An unusual spike of 'polio-like' cases reported in 2012 in California was an early occurrence of what was subsequently defined as AFM.
source: Retrospectively, it now appears, an unusual spike of 'polio-like' cases reported in 2012 in California (Ayscue et al., 2014) was an early occurrence of what was subsequently defined as AFM.
evidence: This retrospective interpretation is supported by citation to Ayscue et al., 2014.

claim: AFM cases have been reported in the UK and elsewhere in Europe in recent years associated with upsurges in EV-D68 detections.
source: In the UK and elsewhere in Europe, AFM cases have also been reported in recent years associated with upsurges in EV-D68 detections (Knoester et al., 2019; The United Kingdom Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) Task Force, 2019; Williams et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Knoester et al., 2019, UK AFP Task Force 2019, and Williams et al., 2016.

claim: Evidence that EV-D68 is the main cause of AFM outbreaks has been growing.
source: Evidence that EV-D68 is the main cause of these AFM outbreaks has been growing (Park et al., 2021; Messacar et al., 2018), although the role of other enterovirus serotypes such as enterovirus A71 (EV-A71) has not been discounted (McKay et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Park et al., 2021 and Messacar et al., 2018.

claim: The role of other enterovirus serotypes such as enterovirus A71 (EV-A71) in AFM has not been discounted.
source: Evidence that EV-D68 is the main cause of these AFM outbreaks has been growing (Park et al., 2021; Messacar et al., 2018), although the role of other enterovirus serotypes such as enterovirus A71 (EV-A71) has not been discounted (McKay et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McKay et al., 2018.

claim: There is no effective treatment or vaccine for EV-D68 infection yet.
source: There is no effective treatment or vaccine for EV-D68 infection yet, and residual paralysis and neurological sequelae after AFM is common and lifelong.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge about therapeutic options.

claim: Residual paralysis and neurological sequelae after AFM is common and lifelong.
source: There is no effective treatment or vaccine for EV-D68 infection yet, and residual paralysis and neurological sequelae after AFM is common and lifelong.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about AFM outcomes.

claim: Many EV-D68 infections are asymptomatic or mild and self-limiting.
source: As for other enterovirus serotypes, many EV-D68 infections are asymptomatic or mild and self-limiting.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about EV-D68 infection characteristics.

claim: Enterovirus surveillance is passive in most countries, based on laboratory reporting for samples submitted by clinicians for testing.
source: In addition, enterovirus surveillance is passive in most countries, based on laboratory reporting for samples submitted by clinicians for testing.
evidence: This describes the general state of enterovirus surveillance systems.

claim: EV-D68 circulation has shown biennial cycles in the US at the national level since 2014.
source: A recent study based on data from the BioFire FilmArray Respiratory Panel (Meyers et al., 2020) has shown biennial cycles of EV-D68 circulation in the US at the national level since 2014, coinciding with the years of AFM outbreaks (Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Meyers et al., 2020 and Park et al., 2021.

claim: Biennial cycles of EV-D68 circulation in the US coincide with the years of AFM outbreaks.
source: A recent study based on data from the BioFire FilmArray Respiratory Panel (Meyers et al., 2020) has shown biennial cycles of EV-D68 circulation in the US at the national level since 2014, coinciding with the years of AFM outbreaks (Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This temporal association is supported by citation to Park et al., 2021.

claim: Reported EV-D68 virus detections in the UK show a biennial pattern between 2014 and 2018.
source: Similarly, in the UK, reported EV-D68 virus detections also show a biennial pattern between 2014 and 2018 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Respiratory samples or throat swabs are infrequently tested by enterovirus surveillance programmes in the US, the UK or elsewhere.
source: However, these data are limited before 2014 and respiratory samples or throat swabs are infrequently tested by enterovirus surveillance programmes in the US, the UK or elsewhere.
evidence: This describes limitations of surveillance systems.

claim: Seroprevalence data from serum samples collected in England in 2006, 2011, and 2017 were used to measure EV-D68-specific neutralising antibodies.
source: To investigate potential changes in virus transmissibility or population susceptibility, we measured the seroprevalence of EV-D68-specific neutralising antibodies in serum samples collected in England in 2006, 2011, and 2017.
evidence: This describes the data collection for the study.

claim: At each time point, seroprevalence slightly decreases from the 0 years-old to the 1–4 yo age classes, and then increases sharply with age until the 20–29 yo, when it reaches a plateau.
source: At each time point, irrespective of the cut-off antibody titre chosen to define seropositivity, seroprevalence slightly decreases from the 0 years-old (yo) to the 1–4 yo age classes, and then increases sharply with age until the 20–29 yo, when it reaches a plateau (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This pattern is observed in the data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Higher seroprevalence values in the 0-yo age class are likely the result of the presence of transplacentally acquired maternal antibodies that subsequently decline.
source: As for many other viruses, higher values in the 0-yo age class are likely the result of the presence of transplacentally acquired maternal antibodies that subsequently decline.
evidence: This is an inference based on known patterns for other viruses.

claim: For a seropositivity cut-off of 1:16, the proportion seropositive at ages 1–4 yo ranged between 0.65 (95% CI 0.54–0.75) in 2006 and 0.92 (95% CI 0.84–0.97) in 2017.
source: For a seropositivity cut-off of 1:16, the proportion seropositive at ages 1–4 yo ranged between 0.65 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.54–0.75) in 2006 and 0.92 (95% CI 0.84–0.97) in 2017.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the seroprevalence data.

claim: For a seropositivity cut-off of 1:64, the proportion seropositive at ages 1–4 yo decreased to 0.29 (95% CI 0.19–0.40) in 2006 and 0.51 (95% CI 0.40–0.62) in 2017.
source: For a more stringent cut-off of 1:64, the proportion seropositive in this age group decreased to 0.29 (95% CI 0.19–0.40) in 2006 and 0.51 (95% CI 0.40–0.62) in 2017.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the seroprevalence data.

claim: Age-stratified seroprevalence was generally lower in 2006 compared to 2011 and 2017.
source: Age-stratified seroprevalence was generally lower in 2006 compared to 2011 and 2017, which suggests individuals acquired their first infection at a lower age through the study period, leading to a decrease in the mean age of exposure.
evidence: This is observed in the data and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The decrease in mean age of exposure could potentially be consistent with increased transmission.
source: This could potentially be consistent with increased transmission (e.g. through increased viral fitness or the accumulation of susceptible) or other mechanisms (such as a change in the virus to have a higher tendency to infect children).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed pattern.

claim: For the 1:16 cut-off, seroprevalence in children <1 month of age starts at 92%.
source: For both cut-offs, seroprevalence in these children starts very high (92% and 70% for the 1:16 and 1:64 cut-offs, respectively, for children <1 month of age) and declines with age, with a quicker decline during the first 3 months of life then followed by a plateau or slower decline.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: For the 1:64 cut-off, seroprevalence in children <1 month of age starts at 70%.
source: For both cut-offs, seroprevalence in these children starts very high (92% and 70% for the 1:16 and 1:64 cut-offs, respectively, for children <1 month of age) and declines with age, with a quicker decline during the first 3 months of life then followed by a plateau or slower decline.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Seroprevalence in infants declines with age, with a quicker decline during the first 3 months of life then followed by a plateau or slower decline.
source: For both cut-offs, seroprevalence in these children starts very high (92% and 70% for the 1:16 and 1:64 cut-offs, respectively, for children <1 month of age) and declines with age, with a quicker decline during the first 3 months of life then followed by a plateau or slower decline.
evidence: This pattern is observed in the data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: For the 1:16 cut-off, seroprevalence reaches a minimum at 8 months of age.
source: Seroprevalence reaches a minimum at 8 and 4 months of age for the 1:16 and 1:64 cut-offs, respectively.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: For the 1:64 cut-off, seroprevalence reaches a minimum at 4 months of age.
source: Seroprevalence reaches a minimum at 8 and 4 months of age for the 1:16 and 1:64 cut-offs, respectively.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The minimum seroprevalence for the 1:16 cut-off remains high at 50%.
source: However, the minimum seroprevalence remains high at 50% for the 1:16 cut-off, compared to only 11% for the 1:64.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The minimum seroprevalence for the 1:64 cut-off is 11%.
source: However, the minimum seroprevalence remains high at 50% for the 1:16 cut-off, compared to only 11% for the 1:64.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Model 2 (random walk model) was the best model according to the leave-one-out (LOO) information criterion for both seropositivity cut-offs.
source: For both seropositivity cut-offs, Model 2 was the best model according to the leave-one-out (LOO) information criterion (see Materials and methods), which accounts for over-parameterisation (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is based on statistical model comparison using LOO criterion.

claim: Model 2 provided a better fit to the data than Model 1.
source: Model 2 also provided a better fit to the data (Figure 2) than Model 1, which did not capture the observed general increase in seroprevalence between 2006 and 2011 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing model fits shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Model 1 did not capture the observed general increase in seroprevalence between 2006 and 2011.
source: Model 2 also provided a better fit to the data (Figure 2) than Model 1, which did not capture the observed general increase in seroprevalence between 2006 and 2011 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The best model (Model 2) estimated an increase in transmission over time during the study period (2006–2017) for both seropositivity cut-offs.
source: The best model (Model 2) estimated an increase in transmission over time during the study period (2006–2017) for both seropositivity cut-offs, as shown by the estimated FOI in Figure 3A.
evidence: This is shown by the estimated FOI in Figure 3A.

claim: For the cut-off of 1:16, the FOI continued to increase until the end of the study period, in 2017.
source: For the cut-off of 1:16, the FOI continued to increase until the end of the study period, in 2017.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For the more stringent cut-off of 1:64, the FOI plateaued from around 2011.
source: However, for the more stringent cut-off of 1:64, the FOI plateaued from around 2011.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The estimated median duration of seropositivity due to the presence of maternal antibodies is 4.9 (95% CrI 3.3–7.2) months for the 1:64 cut-off.
source: We estimated a quicker decline of maternal antibodies for the more stringent cut-off (1:64), with an estimated median duration of seropositivity due to the presence of maternal antibodies of 4.9 (95% CrI 3.3–7.2) months compared to 17.6 (95% CrI 11.5–26.8) months for the 1:16 cut-off (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is estimated from the model and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The estimated median duration of seropositivity due to the presence of maternal antibodies is 17.6 (95% CrI 11.5–26.8) months for the 1:16 cut-off.
source: We estimated a quicker decline of maternal antibodies for the more stringent cut-off (1:64), with an estimated median duration of seropositivity due to the presence of maternal antibodies of 4.9 (95% CrI 3.3–7.2) months compared to 17.6 (95% CrI 11.5–26.8) months for the 1:16 cut-off (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is estimated from the model and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For the 1:64 cut-off, 2.3% (95% CrI 0.4–7.4%) of 1 year-olds are seropositive due to the presence of maternal antibodies.
source: Assuming 90% of individuals are born with maternally acquired antibodies for the 1:64 cut-off, this results in a proportion of only 2.3% (95% CrI 0.4–7.4%) of individuals being seropositive due to the presence of maternal antibodies among the 1 yo, compared to 36% (95% CrI 21–51%) for the 1:16 cut-off and 100% of individuals assumed to be born seropositive.
evidence: This is calculated from the model estimates.

claim: For the 1:16 cut-off, 36% (95% CrI 21–51%) of 1 year-olds are seropositive due to the presence of maternal antibodies.
source: Assuming 90% of individuals are born with maternally acquired antibodies for the 1:64 cut-off, this results in a proportion of only 2.3% (95% CrI 0.4–7.4%) of individuals being seropositive due to the presence of maternal antibodies among the 1 yo, compared to 36% (95% CrI 21–51%) for the 1:16 cut-off and 100% of individuals assumed to be born seropositive.
evidence: This is calculated from the model estimates.

claim: For the 1:16 cut-off, the overall seroprevalence in 2006 was 91% (95% CrI 89–93).
source: For the two seropositivity cut-offs, the overall seroprevalence was already very high in 2006 (91% [95% CrI 89–93] for 1:16 and 70% [66–74] for 1:64, respectively), and continued to increase progressively until 2017, reaching 97% (96–98%) and 87% (85–89%), respectively, for the 1:16 and 1:64 cut-offs.
evidence: This is reconstructed from the model using population age structure data.

claim: For the 1:64 cut-off, the overall seroprevalence in 2006 was 70% (95% CrI 66–74).
source: For the two seropositivity cut-offs, the overall seroprevalence was already very high in 2006 (91% [95% CrI 89–93] for 1:16 and 70% [66–74] for 1:64, respectively), and continued to increase progressively until 2017, reaching 97% (96–98%) and 87% (85–89%), respectively, for the 1:16 and 1:64 cut-offs.
evidence: This is reconstructed from the model using population age structure data.

claim: For the 1:16 cut-off, the overall seroprevalence in 2017 was 97% (95% CrI 96–98).
source: For the two seropositivity cut-offs, the overall seroprevalence was already very high in 2006 (91% [95% CrI 89–93] for 1:16 and 70% [66–74] for 1:64, respectively), and continued to increase progressively until 2017, reaching 97% (96–98%) and 87% (85–89%), respectively, for the 1:16 and 1:64 cut-offs.
evidence: This is reconstructed from the model using population age structure data.

claim: For the 1:64 cut-off, the overall seroprevalence in 2017 was 87% (95% CrI 85–89).
source: For the two seropositivity cut-offs, the overall seroprevalence was already very high in 2006 (91% [95% CrI 89–93] for 1:16 and 70% [66–74] for 1:64, respectively), and continued to increase progressively until 2017, reaching 97% (96–98%) and 87% (85–89%), respectively, for the 1:16 and 1:64 cut-offs.
evidence: This is reconstructed from the model using population age structure data.

claim: For both seropositivity cut-offs, the 2-yo age class has the highest annual incidence of infection.
source: For both seropositivity cut-offs, the 2-yo age class has the highest annual incidence of infection.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The increase in the FOI between 2006 and 2017 results in an increase in the number of infections in the youngest age classes over time, and a decrease in the oldest, with an inflection point around the age of 4–6 yo.
source: The increase in the FOI between 2006 and 2017 results in an increase in the number of infections in the youngest age classes over time, and a decrease in the oldest, with and inflection point around the age of 4–6 yo.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: For the 1:16 cut-off, the mean age at infection decreased from 8.5 yo (7.0–10.4) in 2007 to 4.2 yo (3.5–5.1) in 2017.
source: This, in turn, results in a decrease in the mean age at infection from 8.5 yo (7.0–10.4) in 2007 to 4.2 yo (3.5–5.1) in 2017 for the 1:16 cut-off, and from 14.3 yo (12.9–15.9) to 9.8 yo (8.9–10.8) for the 1:64.
evidence: This is calculated from the model estimates and shown in the insets of Figure 5C.

claim: For the 1:64 cut-off, the mean age at infection decreased from 14.3 yo (12.9–15.9) in 2007 to 9.8 yo (8.9–10.8) in 2017.
source: This, in turn, results in a decrease in the mean age at infection from 8.5 yo (7.0–10.4) in 2007 to 4.2 yo (3.5–5.1) in 2017 for the 1:16 cut-off, and from 14.3 yo (12.9–15.9) to 9.8 yo (8.9–10.8) for the 1:64.
evidence: This is calculated from the model estimates and shown in the insets of Figure 5D.

claim: The model-based analysis suggests an increase in transmission of EV-D68 that occurred or started before 2011.
source: The model-based analysis of individual serological data for EV-D68 from three time points (2006, 2011, and 2017) in England presented here suggests an increase in transmission of EV-D68 that occurred or started before 2011.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the modeling analysis.

claim: The timing of increased EV-D68 transmission coincides with the increased number of outbreaks of EV-D68-associated severe respiratory diseases reported worldwide since the late 2000s.
source: This coincides with the increased number of outbreaks of EV-D68-associated severe respiratory diseases reported worldwide since the late 2000s (Pons-Salort et al., 2015; Tokarz et al., 2012).
evidence: This temporal association is supported by citations to Pons-Salort et al., 2015 and Tokarz et al., 2012.

claim: The results of an increase in FOI over the study period are robust to the choice of the seropositivity cut-off.
source: Although our results of an increase in FOI over the study period are robust to the choice of the seropositivity cut-off, we find striking differences in terms of the magnitude of the FOI and the decline of maternal antibodies depending on the seropositivity cut-off used.
evidence: This is based on comparing results from different cut-offs.

claim: There are striking differences in the magnitude of the FOI and the decline of maternal antibodies depending on the seropositivity cut-off used.
source: Although our results of an increase in FOI over the study period are robust to the choice of the seropositivity cut-off, we find striking differences in terms of the magnitude of the FOI and the decline of maternal antibodies depending on the seropositivity cut-off used.
evidence: This is observed by comparing results from different cut-offs.

claim: The results obtained with the more stringent cut-off of 1:64 seem more realistic for the estimated annual probabilities of infection.
source: The results obtained with the more stringent cut-off of 1:64 seem more realistic, both for the estimated annual probabilities of infection (range 0.32–0.52 for the 1:16, and 0.13–0.20 for the 1:64, for the period 2006–2017) and rate of decline of maternal antibodies (average duration of maternal antibodies around 18 mo for the 1:16, and 5 mo for the 1:64).
evidence: This is the authors' judgment based on biological plausibility.

claim: For the 1:16 cut-off, the estimated annual probability of infection ranged from 0.32 to 0.52 for the period 2006–2017.
source: The results obtained with the more stringent cut-off of 1:64 seem more realistic, both for the estimated annual probabilities of infection (range 0.32–0.52 for the 1:16, and 0.13–0.20 for the 1:64, for the period 2006–2017) and rate of decline of maternal antibodies (average duration of maternal antibodies around 18 mo for the 1:16, and 5 mo for the 1:64).
evidence: This is calculated from the model estimates.

claim: For the 1:64 cut-off, the estimated annual probability of infection ranged from 0.13 to 0.20 for the period 2006–2017.
source: The results obtained with the more stringent cut-off of 1:64 seem more realistic, both for the estimated annual probabilities of infection (range 0.32–0.52 for the 1:16, and 0.13–0.20 for the 1:64, for the period 2006–2017) and rate of decline of maternal antibodies (average duration of maternal antibodies around 18 mo for the 1:16, and 5 mo for the 1:64).
evidence: This is calculated from the model estimates.

claim: The analysis with the 1:64 cut-off infers that there has not been significant changes in the FOI since 2011.
source: Furthermore, the analysis with the 1:64 cut-off infers that there has not been significant changes in the FOI since 2011; however, with the 1:16 cut-off, the FOI continues to increase until 2017.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Most EV-D68 seroepidemiology studies published to date present results for a cut-off of 1:8 or 1:16.
source: That said, most EV-D68 seroepidemiology studies published to date present results for a cut-off of 1:8 (as classically used for polioviruses) or 1:16 (Karelehto et al., 2019; Harrison et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2018a; Xiang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A cut-off of 1:8 is classically used for polioviruses.
source: That said, most EV-D68 seroepidemiology studies published to date present results for a cut-off of 1:8 (as classically used for polioviruses) or 1:16 (Karelehto et al., 2019; Harrison et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2018a; Xiang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established practice.

claim: Only one study has reported detailed seroprevalence in children <1 year old.
source: Only one study has reported detailed seroprevalence in the <1 yo (Sun et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2018b.

claim: A study conducted in China in 2010 found 100% seroprevalence in neonates for a seropositivity cut-off of 1:8.
source: This study was conducted in China in 2010, and the data reported are for a seropositivity cut-off of 1:8. Although they found 100% seroprevalence in neonates, close to the observations in our study when using the 1:16 cut-off, this declined to only 28% in the 9–11 months old, which is much lower than the 64% in the same age class in our dataset (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is from Sun et al., 2018b study.

claim: The China 2010 study found seroprevalence declined to 28% in 9–11 months old children.
source: This study was conducted in China in 2010, and the data reported are for a seropositivity cut-off of 1:8. Although they found 100% seroprevalence in neonates, close to the observations in our study when using the 1:16 cut-off, this declined to only 28% in the 9–11 months old, which is much lower than the 64% in the same age class in our dataset (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is from Sun et al., 2018b study compared to the current study's data.

claim: The increase in transmission is mostly driven by an increase in the total number of infections in children aged 1–5 yo.
source: However, the reconstructed annual number of new infections in each age class suggests that this increase is mostly driven by an increase in the total number of infections in children aged 1–5 yo.
evidence: This is inferred from the reconstructed infection data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Increased transmission in the youngest age groups may be consistent with observed data showing higher and increasing numbers of respiratory illnesses associated with EV-D68 in children <5 yo.
source: Increased transmission in the youngest age groups may be consistent with observed data showing higher and increasing numbers of respiratory illnesses associated with EV-D68 in these age groups (<5 yo) (Bubba et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bubba et al., 2020.

claim: AFM cases do not exclusively or predominantly occur in the youngest age groups.
source: Second, AFM cases do not exclusively or predominantly occur in the youngest age groups.
evidence: This is supported by multiple examples of AFM case age distributions from different countries.

claim: In the US, AFM cases reported in 2014 had a median age of 7.1 yo (interquartile range [IQR], 4.8–12.1 yo).
source: In the US, for example, AFM cases reported in 2014 had a median age of 7.1 yo (interquartile range [IQR], 4.8–12.1 yo) (Sejvar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sejvar et al., 2016.

claim: In the UK in 2018, 40 AFM cases were reported, of which only 22 were 0–5 yo.
source: In the UK, a study from 2018 reported 40 cases, of which only 22 were 0–5 yo (The United Kingdom Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) Task Force, 2019).
